With the arrival of the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro counterpart, Apple has quietly removed one of the most appealing features of this computer. While the two new Mac mini models look almost identical to their predecessors, Apple removed a hidden feature that made the previous-generation Mac mini extremely good value for money.

When the M4 Mac mini first launched, its value was astonishing. It not only came with Apple's M4 SoC, but also featured 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and an Ethernet port. At a retail price of $599 or a student price of $499, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple's lineup, but also the best value per dollar across the entire lineup.

Video: Apple removed the Mac mini's best hidden feature :(

However, Apple's smallest Mac had a hidden trump card that took its appeal to the next level: it had built-in storage upgrade slots. Users could pry open the back cover, remove a few screws, and access a removable NAND module, making it easy to swap in third-party SSDs of up to 2TB.

The benefits were multifaceted. Not only could users upgrade their SSD or easily repair it in the event of a drive failure, but they could also purchase more affordable third-party SSDs, saving considerably more compared to Apple's official upgrade options.

At the time, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade option at $800, meaning this computer marketed as "affordable" would suddenly jump to $1,400 with that one option alone. By buying the base model from Apple and then upgrading with a third-party SSD, users could save nearly $500.

As a DIY enthusiast, I was naturally extremely excited about this, and even filmed a complete tutorial video demonstrating how to upgrade the original SSD with a third-party drive. That video took off incredibly quickly, and has now amassed over 500,000 views.

Video: How to upgrade the M4 Mac mini SSD

However, the good times were not to last.

In the new generation of Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly onto the logic board, essentially eliminating the possibility for users to upgrade it themselves with third-party NAND modules after purchase.

A Mac once widely hailed as the king of value for money has now become a much more expensive product, with the entry-level model jumping from $600 to $900, and the 2TB upgrade option rising from $800 to $1,000.

Currently, if you want to buy an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB SSD, you need to pay Apple $1,900. As for an M4 Mac mini equipped with an aftermarket 2TB upgrade, including the aftermarket upgrade cost of around $320 at the time, the total cost is approximately $920. Of course, overall pricing has generally risen, and this is not entirely Apple's fault (we all understand the reasons), but a price difference of a full $1,000 is by no means purely due to Apple significantly raising prices—it is because Apple eliminated the possibility for users to upgrade themselves.

I can understand to some extent that Apple raised the Mac mini entry price by $300; I can also understand that SSD prices have risen significantly. Chips, SSDs, and memory have all seen cost increases due to AI and other factors. However, this still cannot explain why Apple chose to solder the SSD onto the logic board rather than continuing the previous user-replaceable design.

We can speculate, but the real reason Apple decided to revert to soldered SSDs may never be known. The only certainty is that the pricing of these machines has risen dramatically—to the point where using the word "dramatically" might even be an understatement. Comparing an M4 Mac mini equipped with an aftermarket 2TB upgrade to an M6 Mac mini with a factory 2TB upgrade, the latter costs a full 106% more.

9to5Mac Opinion

It may be somewhat difficult to find an entry-level M4 Mac mini at a reasonable price on the second-hand market, but if you happen to find one, with its solid performance, full-featured design, and upgradeable SSD, it remains an outstanding computer.

On the bright side, all Mac mini models come equipped with Thunderbolt ports, allowing you to easily connect high-bandwidth external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. Personally, I am a huge fan of the Samsung T9, which provides additional storage at a relatively affordable price.

What do you think is the reason Apple removed the user-replaceable SSD design from the Mac mini? Do you have any specific theories? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
